meeting_header: Date: 2026-08-19, Start: 15:00 UTC, Duration: 42 minutes. Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Jin Park (Redwood SE), Maya Lopez (Redwood Solutions Eng), Alex Moreno (Head of ML, Zeppelin AI), Priya Singh (Infra Lead), Jordan Blake (SRE), Eva Chen (CTO - listening in). Recording: Full call.
summary: Discovery / POC scoping focused on capacity sizing and autoscale strategies. Customer goal: validate reserved GPUs + burst capability for production traffic, ensure graceful fallback during capacity shortages, and measure cost/latency tradeoffs. Action items: Redwood to run synthetic bench, send pricing, customer to share workload traces and confirm success criteria. Timeline: initial POC bench in ~2 weeks, pilot (reserved capacity) if success criteria met within month.
topics: Success criteria (latency P50/P95, cost per 1k tokens, error budget)
Workload sizing: concurrency patterns, token lengths, KV cache hit rates
Benchmarks: representative model, quantization, synthetic vs replayed traffic
Reserved GPUs vs hosted burst: pricing and guarantees
Fallback policies: model variant fallback, queueing, rate-limited degraded mode
Security and compliance signals: SOC2, SSO, KMS requirements
Operational observability: tracing, per-request cost breakdown, token-level logs
transcript:
[00:00] Samir: Hey everyone thanks for joining, i think we have about 40 minutes, um quick intros?
[00:06] Alex: Alex here, head of ML at Zeppelin, thanks for arranging. We're trying to scope a POC for production inference.
[00:11] Priya: Priya, infra lead - i'll own the traffic traces and env details.
[00:15] Jordan: Jordan, SRE - i'll be focused on reliability and fallback.
[00:19] Samir: Awesome. Jin, quick intro?
[00:22] Jin: Jin Park, SE, I'll lead the bench and the runtime mapping.
[00:26] Maya: Maya Lopez, solutions eng, i'll document configs and runbook.
[00:30] Samir: Cool. Quick summary of what Zeppelin wants: reliable 99.9 style availability for inference with predictable latency at peak, but cost sensitivity. You're considering reserved GPUs with burst capacity, yes?
[00:45] Alex: Yeah, exactly. Our product has peak windows - user queries spike about 3x for 10-15 minutes during events. We need to avoid tail latency cliffs and want a fallback plan if burst fails.
[00:57] Priya: We also have data residency constraints in EU for some workloads, so region placement matters.
[01:03] Samir: Noted. On the POC we usually validate three things: 1) sizing — does the reserved pool hit your throughput/latency SLOs, 2) burst behavior — can we handle intermittent spikes via burst GPUs, and 3) graceful degradation — how app behaves when capacity limited.
[01:19] Alex: That matches. Success criteria i'd propose: P50 < 120ms, P95 < 500ms on our 2B-ish model, error rate < 0.5%, and cost target under our current infra baseline by 10-15%.
[01:33] Jordan: Also add recovery time objective for capacity failure—like how long to fallback to queued or lower-capacity model. We want <30s for automated fallback.
[01:41] Jin: Got it. For the bench we'll need a representative model binary, token-length distribution, and concurrency histogram. Priya, can you provide a week of traces?
[01:51] Priya: Yes we'll put that in the shared folder. Expect to scrub PII but the token lengths and timestamps are fine.
[01:57] Samir: Great. On sizing: based on your notes so far, the starting reserved configuration we usually recommend is N GPUs sized to handle 80% of expected peak sustained QPS, with burst pool to hit the 3x spike. For your 2B quantized model, quick estimate - one A10s-equivalent handles ~20 RPS at 256 tokens with batching; so we'll map from your trace. That's approximate.
[02:18] Alex: Wait you said A10 equivalent - we generally run on Ampere A10G nodes in our infra. Are those the right comparators, and what about quantization differences?
[02:26] Jin: Right, performance shifts with quant and kernels. If you're running 8-bit (int8) quant, you can get 1.5-2x token throughput. We'll benchmark your artifact to pick kernel and quant profile.
[02:36] Samir: Important point: reserved capacity gives you predictable throughput and priority for scheduling; burst relies on burst pool which is subject to availability but we can configure a guaranteed burst allowance in pilot with a soft SLA.
[02:48] Alex: How does fallback look? If burst isn't available, do requests queue, drop, or get downgraded to a smaller model?
[02:54] Maya: Typical pattern we propose: smart routing — try reserved pool first, then burst pool; if both full, route to a cheaper model variant (e.g., 1B quantized) with degraded results and mark response with a 'degraded' header. If routing can't serve within 500ms, return a queued token and a retry suggestion. We can tune thresholds.
[03:14] Jordan: We want health probes and circuit breakers so bad instances don't saturate available slots. How do you detect and evict slow requests?
[03:21] Jin: Runtime uses per-request timeouts and token-based limits; we can configure soft queue lengths and drop policies. Also prefix/KV cache helps: if many requests share context, cache hits reduce load significantly.
[03:32] Alex: Our workload has ~35% session reuse where prompts share a cached context. That should help, right?
[03:38] Jin: Yes that helps a lot — we'll model with KV cache hit rates. Please include estimated cache hit ratio in the trace.
[03:44] Priya: We'll add that.
[03:46] Samir: Bench plan: step 1 - replay a 24h window at scale to see sustained load; step 2 - run synthetic spike tests to validate burst behavior; step 3 - failure injection to exercise fallback. Estimated bench run time: 2-3 days for initial runs, results within 10 working days. Does that timeline work?
[04:03] Alex: Yes that's reasonable. We'll prioritize spike windows.
[04:06] Jin: For spike tests, we want to measure both cold-cache and warm-cache spikes because warm-cache gives much better tail latency.
[04:13] Jordan: Also measure KV cache 'staleness' — if cache entries TTL out during a spike, performance drops.
[04:19] Maya: We'll instrument cache TTLs in the runbook.
[04:22] Samir: On security, you mentioned EU residency - Redwood Private or Dedicated with region pinning is the safer option. For POC we can run hosted with region controls but if you need customer-managed VPC or on-prem, that'll push timeline.
[04:36] Alex: For the POC we'd prefer hosted in EU region but encryption at rest with our KMS key and SOC2 commitments.
[04:42] Samir: We support customer KMS for Private; for hosted we can use BYOK via a managed integration — we'll surface the compliance docs. We'll send SOC2 report and data flow diagram in the follow-up.
[04:53] Priya: Good. Also SSO/SAML for the console and audit logs are must-haves.
[04:57] Maya: We have SAML SSO and token-level audit logs. We'll include retention options.
[05:03] Alex: Back to numbers — can you ballpark cost delta for reserved pool + burst vs fully on-demand? Our finance wants to see if reserved makes sense for the baseline.
[05:12] Samir: Roughly speaking, reserved gives 30-50% cost savings for sustained capacity. The burst add-on is metered; in some cases burst costs slightly more than on-demand due to priority but you pay only when used. Exact delta requires capacity numbers from your traces.
[05:26] Priya: We'll send the traces. We expect a sustained baseline of ~150 RPS and peaks up to 450 RPS for 10-15 minute windows. Token average ~260 per request. Does that change your sizing?
[05:37] Jin: With 150 RPS sustained and 260 tokens, parallelism and batching matter: measured in tokens/sec per GPU, that'll likely need around 8-10 A10 equivalents reserved to cover 80% sustained, then a burst pool of additional 12-16 GPUs for a 3x spike, depending on batchability. We'll confirm after bench.
[05:53] Alex: 8-10 reserved GPUs seems expensive — can we try more aggressive quantization to reduce count?
[05:58] Jin: Yes, if we use 4-bit or advanced GPTQ-like quantization, throughput can increase 2x but quality degradation risk must be validated on your eval sets. We can include output-quality checks in the bench.
[06:10] Alex: We'll provide an eval suite — we want to ensure generation fidelity above an internal threshold.
[06:15] Samir: Perfect. We'll couple perf bench with quality regression tests. If quantized variant drops quality below threshold, we mark fallback to full model.
[06:23] Jordan: Regarding fallback timing — earlier we said <30s to fallback. Do you mean detection + reroute within 30s?
[06:29] Maya: Yes, detection -> routing -> resume within target. In practice routing changes are near-instant, but spin-up of additional reserved capacity takes longer — that's why burst is important.
[06:38] Priya: Is cold-start for a model shard heavy? If we need to spin up additional reserved nodes, what is the startup time?
[06:44] Jin: Cold-start for a full model load is typically 30-90s depending on model size and storage. Warm-prepped kernels reduce this. That's why we recommend a small warm pool or pre-warmed burst buffer.
[06:56] Alex: Ok makes sense. For POC, we'd like to test two configurations: (A) minimal reserved + larger burst, (B) larger reserved + smaller burst. Compare cost and recovery profiles.
[07:08] Samir: Good plan. We'll run both and provide cost projections.
[07:12] Maya: We'll also simulate 'no burst' failure and test degraded-mode UX; return codes, retries, and user messaging.
[07:20] Jordan: Observability: we need per-request tracing, token-level cost attribution, and model-variant tags for rollouts. Is that available?
[07:27] Jin: Yes, Redwood Console exposes per-route traces, token cost breakdown, and you can tag requests with model variant and rollout id. We'll ensure sampling rates are appropriate to avoid cost.
[07:37] Alex: Sampling is fine as long as we can trace failures to model variant.
[07:41] Samir: On the legal side — procurement asked about data retention and audit logs for the pilot. We have retention config and audit export options. We'll include that in the security packet.
[07:52] Priya: Another question: network egress. Our product renders responses in the EU; do you have EU-based egress controls?
[07:58] Samir: Yes region pinning for inference endpoints and egress within EU regions is supported in Dedicated/Private; hosted can also be region-locked in some cases - we'll confirm for POC.
[08:09] Alex: Great. Timeline recap?
[08:12] Samir: Immediate: Priya uploads traces by 2026-08-22. Samir to send pricing + scoped doc by 2026-08-24. Jin runs bench and shares results by 2026-08-26. Decision on pilot reserved capacity by end of month if success criteria met.
[08:26] Alex: Sounds good. Any blockers?
[08:29] Priya: No blockers, only will need an NDA addendum for a deeper security review if we go Private.
[08:34] Samir: Noted — we'll prepare that if required.
[08:37] Maya: Quick technical note - we'll use a replay harness to drive the bench; please label any PII markers so we can drop sensitive fields.
[08:46] Priya: Will do.
[08:48] Jordan: If bench shows KV cache hit rate helps a lot, can Redwood share tuning tips for TTL and shard sizing?
[08:54] Jin: Yep we'll include recommended TTLs and shard strategies; often a slightly higher TTL gives big wins during short spikes.
[09:02] Alex: One more: can we test fallback to a distilled model that you've pre-verified so we don't do on-the-fly model conversion?
[09:09] Samir: We can bring a Redwood-verified smaller model variant and compare quality. If you prefer we can also quantize your model into a fallback variant during bench. We'll coordinate with you.
[09:19] Alex: Ok great.
[09:21] Samir: Cool, we'll summarize and follow up with the benchmark plan and pricing. Anything else?
[09:26] Priya: No, thank you.
[09:28] Jordan: Thanks all.
[09:30] Samir: Thanks, we'll send notes and next steps. End call.

Notes on transcript: occasional word swap and partial overlap in crosstalk, filler words ('um', 'like') present.
